families.s: HSE waste-vehicle, mobile-plant and pedestrian-segregation guidance
families.t: vehicle routes, pedestrian segregation, reversing, mobile plant, slopes, hand sorting, visibility, maintenance and supervision
f: Waste sites use refuse vehicles, lift trucks, excavators, loaders, cranes and other mobile plant.
Pedestrians have been killed or seriously injured after being struck by manoeuvring waste vehicles and plant.
Effective vehicle and pedestrian segregation is a primary control.
Reversing and blind spots should be reduced through layout, routes, visibility aids and controlled operating zones.
Hand sorting with vehicle assistance requires a system that prevents plant entering the protected sorting area.
Skip-loader operations on slopes can create runaway and stability hazards.
Drivers and plant operators require site rules, competence and clear communication.
Vehicles and safety devices should be maintained and checked for the site conditions and work performed.
families.g: Waste-transport risk depends on vehicle and plant mix, routes, visibility, slopes, ground, pedestrian segregation, reversing, competence, maintenance and supervision.

families.s: HSE skip-loader, hookloader and refuse-vehicle lifting-operation guidance
families.t: LOLER, lift planning, container compatibility, weights, exclusion, hydraulic defects, slopes, inspection and maintenance
f: Hoisting mechanisms on hookloaders, skip loaders and refuse collection vehicles are lifting equipment under LOLER.
Lifting operations should be planned so nobody is in the area where they could be struck by the vehicle, container or load.
Container and skip weights vary substantially and should not be assumed.
The lifting equipment, attachment and container should be compatible and within rated capacity.
Hydraulic arms, hoses, fittings, locks and stabilising arrangements require inspection and maintenance.
Slope and ground condition can affect vehicle stability and create runaway risks.
Defects such as ram creep, leakage or damaged components require the equipment to be removed from service.
Operators need competence and a safe sequence for positioning, lifting, tipping, transport and lowering.
families.g: Waste lifting risk depends on equipment type, container, weight, hydraulic condition, locking, ground, slope, exclusion, inspection and operator competence.

families.s: HSE waste-processing machinery, guarding and blockage-clearance guidance
families.t: conveyors, shredders, trommels, crushers, guards, interlocks, isolation, inspection, maintenance and access control
f: Poorly guarded or improperly used machinery causes serious and sometimes fatal waste-sector accidents.
Waste plants may use conveyors, crushers, grinders, shredders, trommels, balers, compactors and palletisers.
Dangerous parts should be protected by suitable fixed, interlocked or other safeguards.
Blockage clearance and cleaning require effective shutdown and isolation.
Emergency stops do not replace guarding or isolation.
Maintenance and inspection should keep safety-critical devices effective.
Access routes, platforms and housekeeping should allow safe observation and servicing.
Training and supervision should cover normal operation, foreseeable jams, defects and restart.
families.g: Waste-machinery risk depends on machine type, feed variability, guarding, interlocks, blockage, isolation, maintenance, access, housekeeping and competence.

families.s: HSE recovered-paper, baler and compactor safe-system guidance
families.t: feeding, guards, interlocks, isolation, container exchange, hydraulic systems, tipping, maintenance and supervision
f: Recovered-paper guidance covers loading, unloading, sorting, balers, compactors, skips and vehicle maintenance.
Baler and compactor feed openings should prevent access to dangerous moving parts.
Interlocked guards or other protective measures should prevent operation when access is possible.
Clear, unambiguous isolation arrangements are required for blockage clearance and maintenance.
Hydraulic, electrical and mechanical energy should be secured before intervention.
Container exchange and vehicle approach require enough space, headroom and controlled positioning.
Damaged pockets, clamps, pins, hoses or pressure systems require correction before use.
Operators and maintenance staff need task-specific instruction, supervision and safe systems of work.
families.g: Baler and compactor risk depends on feed opening, guarding, controls, stored energy, blockage, container interface, hydraulic condition, isolation and competence.

families.s: HSE waste-composting bioaerosol, hygiene and respiratory-risk guidance
families.t: organic waste, compost turning, airborne microorganisms, COSHH assessment, exposure control, cab protection, hygiene and surveillance
f: Micro-organisms can grow on organic waste and become airborne when waste is handled or composted.
Compost bioaerosols are substances hazardous to health under COSHH.
Exposure should be prevented or adequately controlled where prevention is not reasonably practicable.
Assessments should identify areas and activities with the highest bioaerosol generation.
Turning, screening and maintenance can generate significant airborne exposure.
Enclosed vehicle cabs can provide some protection when properly maintained and used.
Controls may include process enclosure, distance, ventilation, cab filtration, hygiene and suitable RPE.
Workers should receive information on symptoms, contamination control and reporting health concerns.
families.g: Bioaerosol risk depends on waste type and age, moisture, process, agitation, wind and ventilation, distance, enclosure, cab filtration, hygiene, RPE and worker susceptibility.

families.s: HSE WEEE, scrap-metal, aerosol and radioactive-source processing guidance
families.t: crushing, shredding, batteries, refrigerants, aerosols, cylinders, radiation monitoring, depollution and emergency response
f: WEEE and scrap processing may use crushing, grinding, conveying, baling and compacting machinery.
End-of-life vehicles require controlled depollution before further processing.
Batteries, refrigerants, fuels and other hazardous components require identification and safe removal.
Aerosol cans and concealed gas cylinders can create fire, explosion and projectile hazards.
Scrap sites should have arrangements for detecting and responding to radioactive contamination.
Radiation procedures should cover characterisation, recovery, temporary storage and disposal of a discovered source.
Hand-held monitoring equipment and trained responders may be required by the assessment.
Processing lines need controls for machinery, dust, fumes, noise, fire and incompatible materials.
families.g: WEEE and scrap risk depends on feedstock, hidden energy and substances, depollution, machinery, radiation monitoring, fire controls, segregation, competence and emergency response.
